item.title: OpenAI：During this red-teaming exercise, we also found a vulnerability that allows for una…
item.description:
During this red-teaming exercise, we also found a vulnerability that allows for unauthenticated remote code execution in Brotli, a widely-deployed compression library included in many pieces of software such as Node.js, Bun, and Envoy.

The flaw could let an attacker run their own code on affected systems by sending or replying with malicious compressed data, without any need to create a user account. That is, an unpatched server that accepts compressed input could be taken over by a malicious client, and an unpatched client that accepts compressed input (such as “curl --compressed”) could be taken over by a malicious server.

This root cause issue was actually fixed in the Brotli source code in February, but it wasn’t known at the time that it gave rise to a security vulnerability and there was no more recent release of Brotli. Since Brotli is built into other software, any software which includes this library needs to take the update too, followed by the users of that software. We disclosed the vulnerability to Brotli and other downstream projects such as Node.js, which released or are currently releasing security updates, and Brotli cut new release versions and published a CVE.

More details on the patch and mitigations below:
https://t.co/Y1Y72aHxrW

item.title: OpenAI：Over the past several months, we have substantially hardened the security of our re…
item.description:
Over the past several months, we have substantially hardened the security of our research training environment. We’ve removed live internet access for all frontier models during training and built an offline world for them to use instead—a cached version of the web where they can still learn to browse, search, and use applications.

On September 20, after a model exploited a DNS misconfiguration to find a way outside of this offline world, we paused frontier training to strengthen containment further. We assembled teams of agents, powered by our most cyber-capable models, and tasked them with finding weaknesses in our research environments.

While they found no route to the internet they could easily exploit while concealing their activity from our monitors, they did find zero-day vulnerabilities, virtual machine escapes, and hardware side-channels for communication between agents. We used their discoveries to further strengthen our defenses and contribute fixes to open-source software.

After strengthening our containment architecture, we resumed our frontier RL training and inference on October 1. We’ve reserved substantial compute for continuous red-teaming, and made high-compute red-teaming part of the safety cases we use to decide whether frontier training and evaluation can proceed securely.

https://t.co/EmEZsFRMcF

item.title: OpenAI：OpenAI models helped researchers—operating as part of our Patch the Planet initiati…
item.description:
OpenAI models helped researchers—operating as part of our Patch the Planet initiative—discover critical security flaws in PHP, an open-source programming language used to run an estimated 70% of websites.

Over the past two months, we led a coalition of maintainers, researchers, and security providers to prepare fixes and protections ahead of disclosure. This duration was necessary because the fix was quite intricate and required a major change to the PHP engine. Every site using PHP can now safely upgrade their version to stay secure, in addition to applying mitigations from various security vendors.

Due to the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this bug to be one of the most impactful vulnerabilities in recent memory. It also marks a new phase, where AI can find security bugs with internet-scale impact.

This is an example of the Defender’s Window in action: to our knowledge, frontier AI was able to find this vulnerability ahead of attackers, giving defenders time to prepare.
https://t.co/TW3jrSbB3f

item.title: OpenAI：In the same mouse-brain dataset, GPT-Rosalind found a possible clue to why TSC2 mut…
item.description:
In the same mouse-brain dataset, GPT-Rosalind found a possible clue to why TSC2 mutations tend to cause more severe tuberous sclerosis than TSC1 mutations.

The two genes work together to regulate mTOR. Yet in one group of cerebellar neurons, disrupting TSC2 changed the expression of dozens of genes, including genes involved in neuronal communication. Disrupting TSC1 had little effect on gene expression in the same cell type.

Existing treatments already target mTOR. Do they reverse these changes, or is there more to TSC2’s role in these neurons?

item.title: OpenAI：GPT-Rosalind surfaced a new lead for drug discovery: could restoring cholesterol tr…
item.description:
GPT-Rosalind surfaced a new lead for drug discovery: could restoring cholesterol transport protect neurons from degeneration?

DCTN1 is a gene linked to Perry syndrome, a rare neurodegenerative disorder. In mouse-brain data, disrupting it increased expression of genes involved in making cholesterol. GPT-Rosalind suggested a possible explanation: cholesterol may not be reaching where neurons need it.

That gives scientists a specific mechanism to test and, if confirmed, a direction for developing new treatments for neurodegenerative disorders.

With @perturbai_tx and @scrippsresearch, a team of thousands of GPT-Rosalind agents worked in parallel, connecting gene-expression results from millions of mouse brain cells with scientific literature in just 32 minutes. We’re now expanding this collaboration to identify new drug targets.

https://t.co/oHdF3ELsMj

item.title: Harrison Chase：this is great deepdive into what a managed harness looks like! some quick t…

this is great deepdive into what a managed harness looks like! some quick thoughts while reading:

- many diff types of agents built on it. doesnt surprise me - a lot of agents look very similar inside these days

- why not use off the shelf? (1) model and provider agnostic), (2) co-build with product teams, (3) own observability stack. I very much agree with points 1 and 3!!! and is something we obviously emphasize at langchain

- "The simplest agent harnesses are truly just a while loop, but when you want to support a wide array of agentic products in production, the responsibility of the harness or framework expands quite a bit" - +100 to this, is why were investing in deepagents so much

- "Using the “sandbox-as-a-tool” paradigm" - the massive trend seems to be going this way (is how deepagents is architected)

- "Supporting non-blocking async agents as the default". we are working on this right now for deepagents! agree is the future

- "The Connectors Service is the standard interface through which agents at Ramp interact with data sources. It centralizes authentication, credential management, access controls, and tool execution behind one API. This allows us to build and maintain integrations once, and reuse them across products." Also very important! and something we're thinking a bunch about for managed deepagents

item.title: Dan Shipper：BOOK REVIEW: Will and Attention, Meghan O'Gieblyn author of God, Human, Animal…
item.description:
BOOK REVIEW: Will and Attention, Meghan O'Gieblyn author of God, Human, Animal Machine

I loved this book. O'Gieblyn writes with an addictive mix of clarity, rigor, literary references, and self-implicating honesty. I tore through it in a few days.

The book deals with her relapse into alcoholism, how the stories we tell about ourselves can both save us and, when they go stale, ruin us, whether we change from the outside in or the inside out, and how and whether we can trust our own desires.

Underneath it's a story about pragmatism. Her initial recovery from alcoholism rested on a pragmatic philosophy: she treated the core tenets of sobriety—faith as "something you do" surrendering her will to a Higher Power that would keep her safe, and even the resolution not to drink—not as capital T truths, but truths she adopted because they worked.

The problem she found is, for one, this creates a gap between your underlying desires and beliefs and your behavior. One that you hope will close eventually, but if it doesn’t can leave you feeling hollowed out and can keep your actual desires and beliefs unexamined. The other problem, of course, is once you start asking whether sobriety is “useful”, you open yourself to another version of the truth: That it might not be.

One of the things I found so striking about this book is how honest she is, without glorifying drinking, about what alcohol gives to alcoholics. For her, it can bring the kind of unification of self that mystics and yogis seek in God and meditation. So at that point, it is easy for the alcoholic to ask, fairly, why alcohol is not “useful”?

It should be clear that even if you’re not an alcoholic these are the kinds of mental gymnastics all of us do to justify and rationalize any number of behaviors or beliefs.

As an admirer of pragmatism I found this to be quite an interesting and mind-expanding line of questioning.

But I also found it interesting that, as far as I can tell, her turn away from pragmatism—away from truths held to because they “worked,” and back toward a vision of truth and goodness as inviolable and untouchable by experience—ultimately seems to rest on pragmatic grounds. Getting sober again, having faith, and treating the resolution not to drink as an unconditional taboo all, in the broadest sense possible, rest on what they do for her: they keep her desires from talking her back into ruin.

item.title: Harrison Chase：had a lot of fun talking with @HarryStebbings about all things ai
item.description:
had a lot of fun talking with @HarryStebbings about all things ai

one line of questioning we went done - vertical vs horizontal agents, and how to build them

im bullish on vertical agents, and i think you can create differentiation (from horizontal agents) in three ways:

1/ context: prompts, skills, tools - all of this is specific to your domain, pretty easy to provide, and gives domain specific context to the agent

2/ harness: harder to tweak than context, but can alter fundemental behavior of the agent

3/ model: hardest to tweak of all, but obviously changes behavior greatly

i think most agent engineers these days are still tweaking 1 and 2 (in that order)

nb: regardless of what layer you tweak at, as the base models change you should revisit your context/harness/model every 3-6 months (and generally remove cruft that is no longer needed)

https://t.co/gmA8oyfxiX

OpenAI and Anthropic weekly recap, week 42 of 2026: Sora revival talks, a hidden recorder at OpenAI, Anthropic's own source control Scion, a solved ECDSA mystery and more

The Information reports OpenAI is in talks to revive Sora through a startup co-founded by Jeffrey Katzenberg and former Sora lead Bill Peebles, with OpenAI taking equity if a deal closes

OpenAI says they found a hidden recording device in an office, used their models to trace it to an employee, and the FBI made an arrest

The Information also reports early OpenAI talks to buy security firm Trail of Bits

ChatGPT now gathers information across open Chrome tabs through OpenAI's extension, and can control them in ChatGPT Work

OpenAI's GPT-6 Pro got faster with better tool use and multiple agents working in parallel

GPT-5.5 is retired from ChatGPT, ChatGPT Work and Codex, API unaffected, and OpenAI's GPT-4o and GPT-4.1 leave the API on January 14, 2027

Anthropic says strengthened defenses against distillation attacks cut what distillers can harvest by 90 to 99 percent

An internal Claude research model at Anthropic solved a 25-year-old mystery about the NIST ECDSA curve seeds, tracing them to a C library random generator seeded with Unix timestamps

Anthropic built Scion, their own source control, and moved their monorepo off git in five months as daily merges went from roughly 2,500 to over 30,000

Claude Code desktop was reworked for many sessions side by side, Code Review is generally available for Claude Team and Enterprise, and Opus 5.5 fast mode left research preview on the Claude Platform

Anthropic reports agent hours passed human hours internally in March, opened a Singapore office, and says Democracy Works voting information comes to Claude ahead of the US midterms, and more
